title: How to be a Loser (Solo Leveling LIES to you)
summary: NH takes apart the viral Solo Leveling and One Punch Man daily routine (100 push-ups, sit-ups and squats plus a 10 km run) as a training program, giving six reasons it fails. He then argues that isekai stories like Solo Leveling sell young men a chosen-one escapist fantasy of instant change instead of effort, and contrasts them with shonen and sports manga where growth comes from years of work.
claims: The Solo Leveling daily quest (100 push-ups, 100 sit-ups, 100 squats, 10 km run) is Saitama's One Punch Man routine, which was a joke, yet people follow it unironically to get jacked
Fictional routines are written by authors with no resistance training experience, so following them gives disappointing results

The routine ignores whole muscle groups: no pull-up or row for the back, nothing for biceps, squats are not enough for hamstrings, and push-ups only partly cover triceps and shoulders, so the physique ends up unbalanced
Big pecs with spaghetti arms is not a good look

Equal reps across exercises makes no sense: 100 bodyweight squats are far easier than 100 push-ups; something like 10 push-ups to 50 squats would be more balanced since legs are stronger and recover faster
Training the same thing every day leaves no recovery, so you train sore and under-recovered, underperform and grow slower
Doing the same reps every day gives identical volume and intensity with no progressive overload; a good program can add or remove volume and keeps raising intensity
Without a rep range a fixed 100 reps is far too hard for a beginner at first and far too easy later, so it never matches your level
For a complete beginner 100 push-ups a day is a lot, and running 10 km on day one is a bad idea; you should ease in
Adherence is the number one principle of any good program; a program not built to help the trainee stick with it is bad
Running every day at full intensity untrained will cause tendon pain in the Achilles, knees and ankles; people he watched doing the Saitama routine got wrist and shoulder pain from 100 daily push-ups
Fitness influencers and calisthenics bros hyped the Saitama routine for views though they never trained that way and knew it was bad
Followers of the Solo Leveling routine report no change after two months
One upside: the routine gets sedentary anime fans off the couch; to actually progress start with a low-volume novice program like his free one
Isekai follows a formula aimed at young men who feel let down: a weak, unpopular man is suddenly made strong, popular and good with women
The male power fantasy is fine and ancient, as with Hercules; men are wired to obsess over improvement, so stories of improvement resonate with them
The chosen-one myth is fiction: in real life nobody gets randomly picked, and becoming special takes sustained effort; few are born into wealth or rare talent
Going from skinny to jacked in weeks is unrealistic; results take months to show and years before people notice you lift
In Solo Leveling training only earns points and the points build muscle, which teaches that slow, strenuous work is not worth it; the real-world magic shortcut is steroids
Young steroid users are popular on social media because they tell impatient young men to trade health and future for size as fast as possible
Shonen is healthier media: Luffy had trained ten years and grows over years of work, and his DBZ generation watched Goku and Vegeta train hard

Modern shonen like Naruto and later One Piece drift toward bloodlines and destiny, which weakens the hard-work message; sports manga like Hajime no Ippo, where the hero improves only by work, are better
Isekai culture breeds apathy: waiting for something magical to change your fate instead of effort
Judging a man's worth by one metric (strength, wealth, status, number of cars) is reductive self-improvement
The MC becomes more sociopathic and resentful as he gains power; isekai heroes are revenge stories and poor role models
The more you get without working for it, the less grateful you are for it
Unintentionally, Solo Leveling depicts predatory, anti-meritocratic capitalism where random birthright rank decides wealth and power
Pursuing self-improvement only as a pursuit of wealth turns you into the people you hate
Glorified solitary grinding can be escapism: if pain and sacrifice are all your discipline is, you are running from your problems instead of becoming comfortable with yourself
Real self-improvement builds on who you are; renouncing yourself entirely is denial, and grind gurus whose whole personality is the grind are empty
Isekai is a palliative that plays on young men's lack of agency: it feels good while consumed but fixes nothing and teaches wrong lessons
In real life even very attractive men still have to make the first move; what separates you from Chad is also charisma and humour, not just looks
Isekai works like porn: it shows the fruit of your desires while keeping you frustrated and coming back
Compared with Berserk, Solo Leveling has no intentional symbolism or philosophy
Escapism is fine in small doses; a good power fantasy should motivate you and push you forward
This body and this life are all you have; ideas of a do-over in another existence keep you stagnant and mediocre
exercises: incomplete stimulus; daily high reps cause wrist and shoulder pain
far easier than 100 push-ups; not enough for hamstrings
part of a joke routine with no progression
